https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cwyl3w.text: Watch: Family escapes home during Colombia earthquake Watch: Family escapes home during Colombia earthquake Close A family captured video of the moment they fled their home during an earthquake in Colombia. Liliana PÃ©rez Ocampo and her family escaped moments before their home was rocked by a 7.4 magnitude quake on Monday. "At first, we thought it was just a mild tremor like the ones that usually happen in Colombia, but when more than 30 seconds passed and everything was shaking harder, we realised it was an earthquake," the mother-of-four told the BBC World Service. Her family, including two young children at school, are safe. "In the end, material things can be replaced," she said. "The most important thing is life, and we have that." With at least 169 people killed, this has been the strongest earthquake to hit Colombia in the 21st Century, according to the country's Geological Service. More on this story. Credit: Courtesy of the author This is a tumultuous time for American Jews. Start with the documented rise in anti-Semitic attacks in North America, Europe, and Australia, even in locales where Jews felt safe. Last December, two gunmen shot up a Hanukkah ceremony at Bondi Beach near Sydney; in March, a gunman rammed a truck full of explosives into a Michigan synagogue with dozens of children inside. (The explosives never detonated.) All this comes amid the fallout from October 7, 2023, and Hamas’s attack on Israeli soldiers and civilians. Many of the families slaughtered lived in liberal kibbutzim, inside a part of 1948 Israel that is undisputed unless you believe any Israeli state is illegitimate. What followed the Hamas pogrom was the Jewish state’s violent, deadly response, continued fighting on the Gaza moonscape—and now the entire Persian Gulf—dividing Jews in Israel and the diaspora. Returning: A Search for Home Across Three Centuries by Nicholas Lemann Liveright, 416 pp. So Nicholas Lemann’s terrific, researched account of his Louisiana family’s history in America and his own Jewish evolution lands at an important time for American Jews. Returning is the Lemann family story of assimilation and material success in America, and the author’s engagement in middle age with rich Jewish observance. It is told with historical rigor but also novelistic detail. Don’t think of this as a Jewish book, but as an American story with relevance beyond the 2 percent who call themselves Jewish. It is a case study in how, in a free country, Americans choose to wear their religious and ethnic identities, and how the majority culture also influences, even bludgeons, those decisions. It’s right up there with memoirs as diverse as Margo Jefferson’s Negroland , her account of growing up Black and privileged in Chicago, or Richard Rodriguez’s very different Hunger of Memory , about his underprivileged childhood and Mexican American identity. It invites comparison with broad Jewish histories, such as Irving Howe’s World of Our Fathers or Stephen Birmingham’s Our Crowd , but, I’d say, also with Richard Wright’s Black Boy and Frank McCourt’s memoirs, even Barack Obama’s Dreams from My Father . We all decide how ethnic or religious we’ll be, just as the outside world sets its parameters about how it sees us and cajoles us. Returning is not a book about current politics. Lemann, the emeritus dean of the Columbia University School of Journalism, illuminates a constant in Jewish life over the three centuries the book covers, and indeed back to its Abrahamic roots: How do we stay safe as a minority? How do we prosper? And how do we navigate our extensive religious dictums within a wider world that has different ideas about pork chops, working on Saturdays, and the divinity of Jesus Christ? But neither is the book apolitical. Lemann submitted a draft of Returning before October 7 but revised it during the tumult that followed. The shockwaves from the heinous attack on Israelis and foreign nationals—not just Jews but Bedouins and Nepalese and Americans as well—reverberated in Lemann’s personal and professional life on Morningside Heights. He cochaired Columbia’s task force on the university and anti-Semitism, a topic of national interest given the encampment of anti-Israel protestors on the campus blocks away from the nation’s media hub. (This may be America’s most thankless job, aside from being chair of the Democratic National Committee.) The report is a very good piece of investigative work and shows a supple understanding of the line between free speech and harassment, which can be blurry. It was personal for him, too, not just because of his late-in-life religious practice. One of his sons was accosted during the months of protests inside and outside of Columbia’s gates. One anti-Israel protester, seeing a flash of Lemann’s son’s Star of David necklace, dubbed him a “dirty Jew,” which shook the young man. Lemann, a familiar name in American letters and especially to Washington Monthly readers, is revealing a very personal side of himself after a life spent as a reporter and someone who, as a young man, identified with the detached journalist narrator in Robert Penn Warren’s All the King’s Men , the great political and southern novel, modeled on Louisiana’s Huey Long. The president of The Harvard Crimson , Lemann was a friend of his New Orleans contemporary Walter Isaacson and a wunderkind editor here at the Monthly before going on to The Washington Post , Texas Monthly , The Atlantic , The New Yorker , and Columbia. He’s authored books on everything from the Black migration north to meritocracy and the SATs to the difficult world of contemporary capitalism to white terrorism during Reconstruction. But despite recurring themes of race and the South, none was memoir, and not every author can pull off the switch from scrutinizing society to self-scrutiny. But Lemann did. When Returning came out earlier this spring, it received deserved praise from The Wall Street Journal , Air Mail , The Forward , and The New York Review of Books . Hugh Hewitt celebrated it on his radio show, and Lemann took center stage at the 92nd Street Y with Jodi Kantor. Oddly, The New York Times seems not to have reviewed it. (While Lemann is a Monthly contributing editor and sits on its board of directors, I should say that we’re friendly but not friends. I didn’t know his kids’ names until I read the book, and we’ve never had a meal, except at large gatherings.) An interesting aside: He doesn’t write much about his tenure at the Monthly . Still, I was grateful that he refreshed my memory of a bit of, as the kids say, problematic rambling from our shared and beloved mentor, Charles Peters, who founded this magazine and offered a taxonomy of the many Jewish editors who have worked here on a scale of being “Jewy Jews”—that is, ranging from assimilated to easily identifiable. Lemann correctly views this observation as a reflection of both Peters’s puckish humor and his Depression-era West Virginia background rather than a revelation of something sinister. (That’s how I took it, too.) On Charlie’s Jewish meter, Lemann was the most Gentile—“practically white,” I would joke with one of my coeditors back in the 1980s. I confess that when I first met Lemann in the Monthly ’s dilapidated offices near Dupont Circle, with his tortoiseshell glasses, preppy mien, big reputation, unlit cigar, and what appeared to be a futuristic Toshiba laptop with orange-glowing DOS text, I had no idea he was a fellow tribesman. Now I know better why. The Lemann family story is about wrestling with, ignoring, and embracing Jewish identity. The story of the Lemanns in America begins with Jacob Lemann, who emigrated from the Rhine towns of western Germany. Like a goodly number of Jewish expats from the region, he makes his way south, in his case to Louisiana and the sugar cane country around Donaldsonville. A peddler, he opens a store, as thousands of other Jews did in the American South and around the country. An adroit businessman, he grows the enterprise and becomes successful. He marries a Catholic woman, Marie Berthelot, who converts and becomes Miriam. So far, so good. One of the more striking moments in the book is Nicholas Lemann reading the R. G. Dun & Company credit reports on his family, housed at Harvard, where he, his father, and his grandfather went to college. (R. G. Dun would become part of Dun & Bradstreet, the famed analysts of corporate finance.) Over time, the credit reports about Jacob and his family enterprise become more glowing. “Success bought respectability,” Lemann notes. In 1848, one credit agent writes of Jacob, “Can’t give him much of a character [reference] as he is a Jew.” Four years later, another Dun agent calls him “a man of good character.” The references glow brighter as Jacob leaves Louisiana in 1856 for New York City, 20 years after his penniless arrival. His son, Bernard, attends a Dutch Reformed school, Collegiate, still one of New York’s elite private schools. The family has a home in Newport, Rhode Island, to boot. But assimilation is not a smooth journey. Bernard is a worldly young man with a deep interest in both Jewish affairs and broader world affairs. He listens to opera. He sees Shakespeare plays. To avoid conscription into the Confederate Army, he takes a long European tour, effectively avoiding the Civil War. When Jacob and Bernard return to Donaldsonville during Reconstruction, the Radical Republican mayor of the town, a Jew and a relative, is murdered, likely by an ex-Confederate who claimed the title. Amid the credit reports and extensive financial records of his family, Nicholas Lemann learns that Jacob owned slaves. He traded them. He used them as collateral. He won them when planters defaulted on the credit his business had extended to them. As a Jew, Jacob Lemann’s origin story, like all Jews, has a little something to do with Pharaohs and bondage and Passover and deliverance by a merciful God. If the contradictions troubled Jacob, there’s no evidence of it. While Jews were never central to the slave trade or slave ownership, a modern calumny, there assuredly were southern Confederate Jews, most notably Judah Benjamin, a U.S. senator and member of Jefferson Davis’s cabinet. Lemann situates the slaveholding Jew within the broader Jewish-American story: These were not men who saw a contradiction between their own experience of persecution in Europe and their willingness to profit from the enslavement of others. Whether that blindness was a function of ambition, the South, or a community so anxious to belong that it adopted loathsome values, Lemann leaves open. But he does not look away, and his willingness to hold his own family to scrutiny is important. For his part, Jacob’s son, Bernard, leads a Jewish life, marrying into another wealthy German-Jewish family. Bernard’s son, Lemann’s paternal grandfather, Montefiore Mordechai Lemann (known to everyone as Monte), decamps Donaldson with his parents, moves to New Orleans, attends Harvard and Harvard Law School, and opens a firm with a law school classmate (a Gentile) whose father serves on the state Supreme Court. Monroe & Lemann becomes one of the city’s top firms. Monte Lemann is an occasional adviser to Franklin D. Roosevelt and a friend of Supreme Court Justice and New Dealer Felix Frankfurter. While he testifies before Congress for the U.S. to admit more refugees from Europe (it didn’t), he nevertheless lives in a hyper-assimilationist world. He also worries about the unwashed eastern European Jewry threatening the genteel German-Jewish world that Jews like the Lemanns had made. Nicholas Lemann writes that his forbearers believed “that Jews could be Jewish in ways that would not strike non-Jews as strange and threatening—that we could join the wider world without being penalized for being Jewish, and without penalizing ourselves by giving up too much of what we were.” The German Jews of uptown New Orleans feared the Jewish rabble: “To combat anti-Jewish prejudice would be to do something about [the unwashed eastern European Jews], not to do something about prejudice.” But people are complicated. Monte was progressive on civil rights, despite having been raised in Donaldson. He chastised Louisiana Senator Russell Long for signing the Southern Manifesto, which vowed to defend segregation. Monte helped push city fathers to hire more Black police, and devoted himself to the historically Black Dillard University. The affluent uptown Jewish New Orleans of Lemann’s youth had peculiar rituals that distanced it from the rest of the tribe, and his family had its own as well. Monte’s son, Thomas Lemann—or “Father,” as he’s called in Returning —was a prosperous attorney who didn’t deny his Jewishness, let alone seek to become a Christian, as many Jews have. He followed his father to Harvard and Harvard Law, and also to Monroe & Lemann. But in the hyper-assimilationist world of New Orleans in the 1950s and ’60s, the grand Temple Sinai on St. Charles Avenue took on the nomenclature and style of WASP houses of worship, adding new meaning to the old joke that the Jews live like Episcopalians and vote like Puerto Ricans. It called its bar mitzvahs “confirmations,” echoing the Gentile culture. Nevertheless, Father found it too Jewish at times. Nicholas’s dad managed to earn a reprimand from the rabbi for celebrating Christmas in grand style—though not religiously, with a suckling pig, no less—and not Hanukkah. They attended Temple annually—on Thanksgiving. And Nicholas dropped out of its Hebrew school before getting “confirmed.” For most of his life, Father had no interest in Zionism or the Holocaust and little interest in the cultural Judaism most of us Ashkenazi (or European) Jews are steeped in. As Lemann writes, “I went off to college, never having tasted any of the familiar Jewish foods: bagels, lox, kugel, matzoh, gefilte fish, latkes, babka, and so on. Many of the foods of my childhood, like gumbo and jambalaya, which still exert an inescapable tug, are triply treyf because they use pork, shellfish, and butter all in the same dish.” No wonder Father hid baskets of kippot or yarmulkes at Nicholas’s wedding and his mother’s funeral. We learn that a persistent fear of being too Jewish haunted Thomas Lemann, of being mistaken for the pushy, eastern European sorts rather than the genteel German extraction. In a touching yet slightly horrifying scene, a young Nicholas becomes the first Jew invited to one of the many elite “Krewe” parties that spring up in the city during Mardi Gras, a famously big deal in Catholic New Orleans, arguably as much a Caribbean city as an American one. Father comes to Nicholas’s bedroom, and the moment is weighty as he implores his son to accept the golden ticket but not to bring any Jewish guests—he’s allowed to bring a couple who will sit in the balcony as the reverie proceeds—because the Gentile hosts, and presumably everyone else, will see it as the aggressive, arriviste trait of the unwashed Jews trying to get more of their own in. It’s Edith Wharton for the Israelites, like the endless obsession with status and manners in The Age of Innocence . We come to see how Thomas, with whom he expresses great sympathy, embraced what Lemann calls this “deracinated” Jewish identity. He was on campus during the drastic retrenchment of Jewish admissions at Harvard as quotas were imposed in the 1940s. And he had a fine-tuned antenna for what was acceptable. He comes across as a wonderful man—bighearted and curious with a penchant for global travel (except to Israel, which he never visited), great art, and good living. And Lemann’s boyhood home had its own name when most of us just had an address. His father called it Quercus, after the Latin name for “live oaks.” They had a butler. But having attended Harvard in the postwar era of Jewish quotas, Father’s anti-Zionism and distancing himself from Jewish life rendered his Jewishness invisible to those who might use it against him. Lemann treats this generational logic with sympathy, but he doesn’t excuse it. The willingness to assimilate, he suggests, came with a price: a kind of spiritual hollowness without real safety. Wight will present on wildlife research, talk about what inspires her characters and their adventures in her books, and offer a fun and active wildlife fact game, according to the Library, in a news release. Books will be available to purchase and have signed (if you have your own copies, you can bring them to be signed). This event concludes the Library's 2026 summer reading program (Plant a Seed, Read!). Summer Reading participants should get their reading challenge sheets in for their prize tickets, said Gibbs. The end-of-program drawings will happen at this event. (Get your tickets in before the library closes at noon on Thursday, September 10.) There will also be door prizes at this event with Wight. "You do not have to be a summer reading participant to attend this event," said Gibbs. "Everyone is welcome!" Tamra Wight and her husband, David, raised two children while running Poland Spring Campground in Poland, Maine, for 28 years. She is a nature geek and wildlife photographer: you'll often find her hiking, kayaking, power-walking, geo-caching, and snowshoeing in hopes of capturing new wildlife behavior through her lens. Wright now lives in Turner, Maine. See www.tamrawight.com for more information. Gibbs Library is located at 40 Old Union Road, Washington, Maine 04574. FMI: 207-845-2663 / info@gibbslibrary.org / www.gibbslibrary.org and check them out on Instagram and Facebook. https://carnegieendowment.org/events/202.text: { "authors": [ "Senator Elissa Slotkin", "Anne Applebaum " ], "type": "event", "centerAffiliationAll": "dc", "centers": [ "Carnegie Endowment for International Peace" ], "englishNewsletterAll": "democracy", "nonEnglishNewsletterAll": "", "primaryCenter": "Carnegie Endowment for International Peace", "programAffiliation": "DCG", "programs": [ "Democracy, Conflict, and Governance" ], "regions": [ "United States", "Central Europe" ], "topics": [ "Democracy", "Civil Society", "Political Reform" ] } Event A Conversation on Defending Democracy With Senator Elissa Slotkin and Anne Applebaum Wed, September 30th, 2026 Washington, DC and Live Online Link Copied Program Democracy, Conflict, and Governance The Democracy, Conflict, and Governance Program is a leading source of independent policy research, writing, and outreach on global democracy, conflict, and governance. It analyzes and seeks to improve international efforts to reduce democratic backsliding, mitigate conflict and violence, overcome political polarization, promote gender equality, and advance pro-democratic uses of new technologies. Learn More Invalid video URL Democracy is under significant threat worldwide, with dozens of established democracies, including the United States, undergoing illiberal turns. Yet amid the global democratic recession, there are also signs of hope. Both Poland and Hungary, which previously experienced substantial democratic erosion, are forging more encouraging paths. What can the United States and other democracies learn from these shifts? Following a recent visit to both countries, Senator Elissa Slotkin has been examining the authoritarian playbook used abroad and the lessons that can be taken to protect institutions and rights in America. Senator Slotkin, who has spent her career at the intersection of national security and public service, serving as a CIA analyst, senior Pentagon official, and now U.S. Senator for Michigan, will share her insights in conversation with Anne Applebaum, a Pulitzer Prize-winning historian and a leading expert on the global rise of autocracy and democratic backsliding. Please join the Carnegie Endowment’s Democracy, Conflict, and Governance Program for this conversation. Light refreshments will be served. United States Central Europe Democracy Civil Society Political Reform Event Speakers Senator Elissa Slotkin United States Senate Anne Applebaum Staff Writer, The Atlantic Carnegie does not take institutional positions on public policy issues; the views represented herein are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of Carnegie, its staff, or its trustees. Event Speakers Senator Elissa Slotkin United States Senate Senator Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) is the junior Senator from Michigan, serving on the Armed Services, Homeland Security, Veterans' Affairs, and Agriculture, Nutrition, & Forestry committees. Before Congress, she worked in national security. She served in the CIA, completing three tours in Iraq alongside the U.S. military. She also held key roles at the Pentagon and White House under Presidents Bush and Obama. Anne Applebaum Staff Writer, The Atlantic Anne Applebaum is a Pulitzer prize-winning historian, a staff writer for The Atlantic and a senior fellow at the SNF Agora Institute at Johns Hopkins University. Her history books include Red Famine: Stalin’s War on Ukraine; Iron Curtain: The Crushing of Eastern Europe 1944-1956; and Gulag: A History , which won the 2004 Pulitzer Prize for non-fiction. Her most recent books are the New York Times bestsellers Twilight of Democracy, an essay on democracy and authoritarianism, and Autocracy Inc: The Dictators Who Want to Rule the World.

Per saperne di più By Andrius Sytas and Terje Solsvik RIGA, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ centrist, pro-Ukraine United List party won Saturday’s parliamentary election by an unexpectedly wide margin, partial results showed, with many voters on edge amid warnings of potential Russian aggression. With 72% of ballots counted, United List was on 36.5%, followed by the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First on 13.0%. Latvia First had courted the country’s substantial ethnic Russian minority in the run-up to the vote. Baltic countries have warned for months that Russia is mounting sabotage, cyber and other hybrid attacks across Europe to erode support for Ukraine and sow fear, although Western officials dismiss concerns that Moscow is capable of launching a direct assault on NATO, of which Latvia is a member. Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria. Reacting to exit poll readings earlier in the evening, Kulbergs said he hoped to remain prime minister but that he would not want to govern with Latvia First. According to partial results, he will still need coalition allies to form a government. “It’s remarkably good. I was not expecting such a result,” Kulbergs said at his party’s headquarters in Riga. Third in the exit poll ranking was the pro-Russian Sovereign Power party, on 10.5%, followed by the nationalist National Alliance, which promotes a hardline approach to the Kremlin, at 9.6%. SHADOW OF UKRAINE WAR A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray military drones flew undetected into Latvia. Though the drones were Ukrainian, officials have blamed Russia for causing them to divert from their flight paths. “The priority, in my view, is, of course, security – security in Latvia,” said Megija Nordena, 21, from Riga. “And then … as a student, I’d say support for students, the economy, and also support for pensioners.” Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs has also promised more anti-drone capabilities for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in NATO. His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and should instead focus more on cost-of-living issues, particularly among the country’s Russian-speaking minority. “Our voters want peace, to stop looking for shelters, to no longer experience the air alerts,” Sovereign Power party leader Julia Stepanenko told Reuters. “The war must not be encouraged in any way, including by financing it … Ukraine must win, but through peace talks.” The ethnic Russian minority in Latvia is split between those who feel embarrassed or angry about the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine, and those frustrated with policies at home aimed at limiting their influence on public life that many see as discriminatory. Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea, and Russia and Belarus to the east, with EU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south. (Editing by Justyna Pawlak, Timothy Heritage, Emelia Sithole-Matarise, Alex Richardson and William Mallard) Di Andrius Sytas e Terje Solsvik RIGA, 4 ottobre (Reuters) - Il partito di centro e filo-ucraino “Lista Unita” del primo ministro lettone Andris Kulbergs ha vinto le elezioni parlamentari di sabato con un margine inaspettatamente ampio, secondo i risultati parziali, mentre molti elettori erano in apprensione a causa degli avvertimenti su una potenziale aggressione russa. Con il 72% dei voti scrutinati, “Lista Unita” era al 36,5%, seguita dal partito populista “Lettonia Prima”, di stampo MAGA, al 13,0%. “Lettonia Prima” aveva corteggiato la consistente minoranza etnica russa del paese nella fase precedente al voto. I paesi baltici hanno lanciato avvertimenti da mesi sulla Russia, che sta orchestrando sabotaggi, attacchi informatici e altre forme di attacchi ibridi in tutta Europa per minare il sostegno all’Ucraina e seminare paura, sebbene i funzionari occidentali respingano i timori che Mosca sia in grado di sferrare un attacco diretto contro la NATO, di cui la Lettonia è membro. La Russia sostiene che tali accuse siano infondate e frutto di un’isteria anti-russa. Reagendo ai dati degli exit poll diffusi in serata, Kulbergs ha affermato di sperare di rimanere primo ministro, ma di non voler governare con «Latvia First». Secondo i risultati parziali, avrà comunque bisogno di alleati di coalizione per formare un governo. «È un risultato straordinariamente positivo. Non mi aspettavo un risultato del genere», ha dichiarato Kulbergs dalla sede del suo partito a Riga. Al terzo posto nella classifica degli exit poll si è classificato il partito filorusso «Potere Sovrano», con il 10,5%, seguito dall’Alleanza Nazionale, di orientamento nazionalista e fautrice di una linea dura nei confronti del Cremlino, al 9,6%. L’OMBRA DELLA GUERRA IN UCRAINA Kulbergs, 47 anni, uomo d’affari e pilota di rally amatoriale, è salito al potere a maggio dopo che la precedente coalizione si era sciolta a causa della gestione degli incidenti in cui droni militari vaganti erano entrati in Lettonia senza essere individuati. Sebbene i droni fossero ucraini, i funzionari hanno accusato la Russia di averne causato la deviazione dalle rotte di volo. «La priorità, a mio avviso, è ovviamente la sicurezza – la sicurezza in Lettonia», ha affermato Megija Nordena, 21 anni, di Riga. «E poi… come studentessa, direi il sostegno agli studenti, all’economia e anche ai pensionati». Durante tutta la sua campagna elettorale, Kulbergs ha anche promesso di potenziare le capacità anti-drone della Lettonia e di mantenere la spesa per la difesa al 5% del prodotto interno lordo, uno dei livelli più alti della NATO. I suoi rivali filo-Cremlino hanno affermato che la Lettonia dovrebbe interrompere qualsiasi aiuto all’Ucraina e concentrarsi invece maggiormente sulle questioni relative al costo della vita, in particolare tra la minoranza di lingua russa del paese. «I nostri elettori vogliono la pace, smettere di cercare rifugi, non dover più subire gli allarmi aerei», ha dichiarato a Reuters la leader del partito Sovereign Power, Julia Stepanenko. «La guerra non deve essere incoraggiata in alcun modo, nemmeno finanziandola… L’Ucraina deve vincere, ma attraverso i negoziati di pace». La minoranza etnica russa in Lettonia è divisa tra coloro che provano imbarazzo o rabbia per la guerra del Cremlino in Ucraina e coloro che sono frustrati dalle politiche interne volte a limitare la loro influenza sulla vita pubblica, che molti considerano discriminatorie. La Lettonia, con una popolazione di 1,9 milioni di abitanti, è situata tra il mar Baltico e la Russia e la Bielorussia a est, con l’Estonia e la Lituania, alleate dell’Unione europea e della NATO, a nord e a sud. Photograph: Hasan Zaidi/Alamy Rights and freedom Global development Woman in Saudi Arabia sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage Rights groups condemn reported punishment of Kenyan migrant worker as an ‘act of violence’ Supported by About this content Deepa Parent Wed 11 Nov 2026 04.15 EST First published on Wed 11 Nov 2026 01.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Kenyan mother in Saudi Arabia has reportedly been sentenced to 100 lashes after giving birth outside marriage. Under the Saudi sharia law system, sex outside marriage is a criminal offence. But it is women who are disproportionately targeted, say rights groups, which have condemned the punishment as an “act of violence”. Although many unmarried women give birth in Saudi Arabia, rights groups say the Kenyan mother’s case only came to light because she had been taken to a hospital, which are required to report single women giving birth to the authorities. “Most of them give birth at home, that’s why they aren’t reported,” said Ekaterina Porras Sivolobova, founder of Do Bold, a non-profit organisation advocating for migrant workers’ rights in the Gulf. The Kenyan mother, Esther Wanja Muthoni, was a domestic worker recruited to work as housekeeper and nanny in Saudi Arabia. She reportedly became pregnant during a brief relationship with an Egyptian man and said that the child’s father had since left the country. A 2024 Guardian investigation found a number of Kenyan single mothers were abandoned by their children’s fathers out of fear of being arrested for having extramarital sex. After the ruling, which was issued last month, Muthoni told the New York Times she was afraid about not being able to endure the lashes and said: “I don’t deserve this.” The case comes as a planned visit to Saudi Arabia by Reem Alsalem, the UN special rapporteur on violence against women and girls, was postponed last week . Alsalem said she had intended to “raise the situation of specific cases during the visit. If the visit does not take place soon, I will do so separately through the established channels that we have as mandate holders.” Kenyan single mothers ‘trapped’ in Saudi Arabia as exit visas denied to children born outside marriage Read more Maryam Aldossari, acting director at the UK-based rights organisation ALQST ( al-qist means “justice” in Arabic), said the ruling was an act of violence and the woman should have been sent back to Kenya and not punished. “It just shows the hypocrisy behind so-called Saudi reform. We know MBS [Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince] has been trying to show the world that Saudi is becoming a modern country that empowers women, yet we see the court sentence a mother to 100 lashes,” said Aldossari. In April 2020, Saudi announced a reform to end flogging as a judicial punishment. However, it only applied to ta’zir offences, where judges have discretion over punishments. Although most flogging sentences fell into this category, flogging remained a possible punishment for certain hudud (fixed punishments under Islamic law) offences, such as alcohol consumption and adultery, ALQST said in a report in 2021. Sivolobova said it had been difficult to help in cases involving Kenyan mothers compared with those from other countries. “I haven’t been able to get help from the Kenyan authorities to support these women,” she said. The Saudi government was approached for comment.
